trained_on: University Student Stress Dataset (Mendeley Data, DOI 10.17632/rc5htd5dfr.1, CC BY 4.0); n=3000 rows after cleaning; seed=42

features.name: Exam_Frequency
features.label: How often do you have exams or tests? (1 = rarely, 9 = very often)
features.help: Your own rating on a 1-9 scale.
features.tip: Put every exam date in MindSync so busy weeks are visible early.

features.name: Assignment_Load
features.label: How heavy is your assignment workload? (1 = light, 9 = very heavy)
features.help: Your own rating on a 1-9 scale.
features.tip: Break big assignments into small tasks with their own deadlines.

features.name: Sleep_Hours
features.label: How many hours do you sleep on a normal night?
features.help: Average over the last few weeks.
features.tip: Regular sleep is one of the most reliable ways to cope with a heavy workload.

features.name: Social_Media_Use
features.label: How many hours a day do you spend on social media?
features.tip: Notice when scrolling replaces a break you actually needed.

features.name: Screen_Time
features.label: How many hours a day are you in front of a screen in total?
features.help: Phone, laptop, TV and games together.
features.tip: Look away from screens for a few minutes every hour.

features.name: Physical_Exercise
features.label: Do you exercise regularly?
features.help: The dataset recorded this as a Yes/No answer.
features.tip: Even a short walk between study blocks can help.

features.name: Family_Support
features.label: How supported do you feel by your family? (1 = not at all, 9 = completely)
features.help: Your own rating on a 1-9 scale.
features.tip: If support at home is low, a friend, tutor or student services can fill part of that gap.

features.name: Anxiety_Level
features.label: How anxious do you usually feel? (1 = calm, 9 = very anxious)
features.help: Your own rating on a 1-9 scale.
features.tip: If anxiety is getting in the way of daily life, please talk to someone you trust or a counsellor.

card.intended_use: Shows which stress-load band a survey scoring rule would give to your answers, and which answers contribute most. A reflection aid for the student, not a prediction of burnout.
card.probability_meaning: Each percentage is how confident the model is that the dataset's own scoring rule would put answers like yours in the Low, Medium or High band. On held-out rows the average gap between stated confidence and how often the model was right (calibration error) was 0.073 (0 would be perfect). It is not the chance that you will burn out, and it was not checked against any real-world outcome.
card.not_for: Medical or psychological diagnosis, grading, or any decision about a person.
limitations: Trained on one dataset described as a survey of undergraduates at universities in Bangladesh; results may not transfer to other countries or courses.
The dataset's stress label is a score the authors computed from the answers. The model learns that scoring rule, not clinically measured stress.

The stress score is an exact formula of the answers and the inputs look like independent, flat random numbers. That pattern is typical of computer-generated data and very unusual for a real questionnaire. It cannot be proven from the file alone (ask the dataset authors). Either way the model has learned the dataset's scoring rule, not independently measured stress.
Questions dropped because they carry no information in this dataset: Study_Hours, Class_Attendance, Peer_Pressure.
Answers are self-reported and the data is a snapshot, so the model shows association, not cause.
Probabilities are model estimates and can be wrong for any individual student.
